findings.message: A different agent (Claude) checked the work in a separate headless process.

The feature, spec and dimensions are consistent with each other. The feature has 12 scenario blocks that compile to 17 cases: R1 has 4, R2 has 6, R3 has 2, R4 has 4 and R5 has 1. This matches the ticket's corrected census. Each of R1–R5 has at least one CLI-surface acceptance example. The examples cover both success and refusal for the main risks: command substitution, dirty inputs, a candidate change mid-run, an unmapped case, absent/skipped/failed required assertions, a runner that fails despite passing assertions, tampered reports, retries that keep earlier attempts, and paired semantic-versus-bookkeeping freshness. Duplicate or ambiguous results, other override kinds, incomplete persistence, count-only impostors and refused-path history preservation are not in the acceptance examples. Instead they are assigned to named lower-level matrices that state concrete conditions that fail when the behavior is broken. Exclusions (certification, closing, shared gates, historical rewriting, the 33 deferrals) are kept and reflected in R5. I found no concrete error. The remaining risks are feasibility and placement questions that the ticket already lists as implementation-planning obligations.

The @demo success scenario and the spec's Success threshold assume a reviewed mapping that supports all 37 T3E4NS cases. proof-map.md's Certification gap says some current registrations may not support this. For fallback order, citing the parameterized test title is not enough: the mapping must cover both declaration orders and the success and failure branches. For route admission, the degraded-labeling/empty-set test is supporting evidence only, not a substitute for the matching-identity, wrong-identity and stale-digest outcomes. If any case is unsupported, R2 requires a named refusal, so the killer demo can never be reached without adding scope, which the spec forbids. Mapping feasibility is already recorded as a planning obligation. Resolve it before committing to the demo, or state explicitly that the demo depends on that review.

R1 requires that a clean, committed change to accepted scope be refused before execution, with a request to review an updated contract. The acceptance examples only show a scope change at verification time (the R4 outline row). The pre-execution case lives only in the lower-level observer-source-identity matrix. That placement is acceptable, but one CLI example would show that this refusal is wired through the public entrypoint and not just the internal checker.

Where observation and attempt records are stored is still undefined. If records or diagnostics are written inside the original checkout (for example, under the ticket directory), they become untracked changes. That can collide with the clean-candidate precondition: the R3 retry scenario retries the 'same clean committed candidate' after a failed attempt was retained. It can also break the R1 claim that the checkout stays unchanged. Implementation planning must either keep these records out of the bound input set and the dirty-check, or store them outside the checkout. The ticket already names storage isolation as an obligation; this is the concrete failure if it is left unresolved.

In the R1 acceptance examples, only command substitution is refused. R1 also lists ticket, report, test-filter and success-flag substitution; those are left to the observer-request-contract matrix. Make sure that matrix includes a substituted known, valid ticket (for example CKWE2D or 5F5ZZA), not only an unknown one.

R5's acceptance example only covers the successful path. dimensions.md extends history-preservation and execution-evidence-only meaning to refused and interrupted outcomes at the lower level. This is consistent with the spec's statement that both successful and refused observations carry that meaning.
